>   Apply to all save operations.

I was going to ask if it shouldn't make more sense to unset the `save_path` variable on any write error, i.e. inside `FileAccess::store_buffer` et al. but looks like that's the plan already?

>  was going to ask if it shouldn't make more sense to unset the save_path variable on any write error, i.e. inside FileAccess::store_buffer et al. but looks like that's the plan already?

While it can be unset in `store_buffer`, and this will prevent overwriting the original file, I prefer to do it where `store_*` is called, since it additionally allows producing more meaningful errors and cancel more complex operations on write error, checking results of `store_*` should be done anyway. Also, not every case should be fully aborted, for something like logs it's better to have it partially written then not written at all.

Gotcha.

A footnote on write error handling: When dealing with raw file write errors (i.e. not compressed, not encrypted writes), errors are often delayed and the underlying API (including std's FILE o fstream) lie. This is because of the highly async nature of IO.

Imagine the following:

1. write 32 bytes - returns success.
2. The underlying OS or disk encounters an error.
3. write 16 bytes - returns failure. However this failure is actually from step 1.

Flushing the descriptor (fflush) can help. However there are many types of failures:

1. File / folder removed. Highly depends on the OS. Probably detected after fflush. Most likely to be spotted when opening the file (due to how most file systems work) rather than on write().
2. Underlying API is out of RAM. IO is probably the least of your problems. Probably the process crashes before the error is successfully reported to the user.
3. Disk removed. E.g. USB cable got yanked out, network share went down, etc.
4. Out of Space - probably detected after fflush, as the usually OS knows this (it may not due to the parallel nature of IO).
5. Bus error - It may not be detected in time, as the OS delays the writeout to disk until it has enough data (or the OS is very far behind because the disk write speed cannot keep up with all the data piled up).
6. Disk Controller error - probably detected much later, as the disk also async returns "everything ok" to the OS but later on reports a physical error. This error may not even be detected at all by the process (e.g. fclose() returned everything ok).
7. In theory full disk sync ensures fully synchronous & accurate error reporting; but that also depends on the drive's firmware. Also full sync on network shares is practically impossible (e.g. Samba / NFS may return "everything ok" but that computer has its own caches to flush).

Flushing excessively is bad for throughput performance and it still doesn't guarantee the error is spotted.

Plus 99.99% of the time it doesn't matter; because what really matters is whether the whole file was written successfully or not. It doesn't matter if the first 10 bytes succeeded but the next 4 bytes did not. There are exceptions such as torrent SW which downloads large data in chunks; backup SW also does care about which bytes are OK. But the general case only cares about the whole file succeeding.

And in almost all cases, the reasons for failure are extremely bad (either out of space which can be really bad if it's the system drive, or a serious HW error).

**This is not a comment saying what you're doing is futile:** I'm just pointing out that you need to have clear what's the goal with the error checks and how obsessive & paranoid you want it to be, and be aware of the issues with IO writes when the code is running in the real world.

Compressed or Encrypted files is a different issue, since there can be a myriad of other errors (it's much more common to run out of RAM, there can be bugs in the encoding process, unsupported data patterns, wrong settings, etc)
